title: Scaffolding Is a Trap
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles, a 34-year classroom veteran, argues that excessive scaffolding is the enemy of complex thinking. Drawing on his own experience and a close re-reading of Rosenshine, he develops a 'whole-part-whole' model of instruction: present the complete task first, work on a small scaffolded component, then return to the full challenge with cognitive overload. He uses driving lessons and swimming instruction as models: minimal scaffolding at the outset, immediate exposure to full-complexity tasks, with mastery following from repeated overload rather than incremental protection. Salles re-reads Rosenshine's Principle 7 (80% success rate) to show it applies to the final mastery check questions—not to practice problems en route—allowing rigorous, high-demand practice throughout. He extends this analysis through Robert Bjork's desirable difficulties: interleaving, spacing, and varied practice produce worse immediate performance but better long-term retention, precisely because they produce productive error without permanent scaffolding. The article applies this framework to English literature tasks: students working on Macbeth need to grapple with the full complexity of a question rather than being protected through scaffolded sub-tasks that fragment the thinking required.
points: * The 'whole-part-whole' model: present the complete complex task first, then isolate a small component for targeted practice, then return to the full task—maximizing cognitive overload and transfer rather than minimizing challenge. * Rosenshine's 80% success rate applies to final mastery check questions, not to practice problems; rigorous, demanding practice can (and should) involve lower success rates, as long as the final mastery check reaches 80% for each student. * Robert Bjork's desirable difficulties (interleaving, spacing, varied practice) produce worse immediate performance but better long-term retention—precisely because they generate productive errors without the crutch of permanent scaffolding. * Scaffolding slows down the development of complex thinking: when the task is always divided into manageable parts, students never practice the cognitive integration that complex performance requires. * Driving instruction and swimming instruction both demonstrate the principle: minimal initial scaffolding followed by immediate exposure to full-complexity performance, with mastery following from repeated demanding reps.
quotes: Tasks need to be simple. But thinking needs to be hard. Thinking needs to be complex. Scaffolding is the enemy of complex thinking.

Here's the whole thing I want you to master first. Ok, let's play around with a part of it - a small scaffold. Right, now let's try a big chunk of the whole thing again, where you will have to connect loads of stuff in addition to the small part I just scaffolded for you. More, more, more. The whole first, little parts next, back to the whole. Overload.
Minimal scaffolding, a lot of cognitive overload. It didn't take long for the arm bands to come off.

Practice, we are told, makes perfect, but practice can be a disaster if students are practicing errors! If the practice does not have a high success level, there is a chance that students are practicing and learning errors.
It makes you feel great as a teacher, because your students are always improving. But are you just filling a bucket, one cupfull at a time? Turn on the tap.
